outcome: Two independent, unpublished 2026 preprints moved bounds on the area of a convex universal cover for Moser's worm problem: Ethan Keller (arXiv:2609.21968, Sept 18 2026) raised the convex lower bound to 0.239 and lowered the convex upper bound to 0.24633..., cutting the gap between previously refereed bounds by over 75%, with the full proof formalized and kernel-checked in Lean 4; Zhipeng Deng (arXiv:2609.04591, Sept 4 2026) separately claims a specific isosceles-triangle convex cover of area 0.257883595..., also Lean-formalized. The overall problem (exact minimum area) remains open, and neither preprint has yet received expert digestion or journal review.
summary: Moser's worm problem — the exact minimum area of a region covering every unit-length plane curve — remains open. Wikipedia's live article (checked 2026-09-22) still lists the best refereed bounds as of the frozen revision's era: convex lower bound 0.232239 (Khandhawit, Pagonakis & Sriswasdi 2013), convex upper bound 0.270911861 (Wang 2006), and nonconvex upper bound 0.260437 (Norwood & Poole 2003) / the 30° sector result of Panraksa & Wichiramala (2021, area π/12≈0.2618, settling Wetzel's conjecture) — all predating the window. Since 26 January 2024, two new, apparently independent single-author preprints have appeared in September 2026 that would move the convex bounds if they hold up: (1) Ethan Keller, 'Improved bounds for universal convex covers of unit arcs' (arXiv:2609.21968, submitted 2026-09-18), claims 0.239 ≤ α ≤ 0.24633..., a combined lower+upper bound improvement cutting the previously refereed gap by over 75%, with the full proof Lean 4-formalized and kernel-verified, code/certificates on GitHub. (2) Zhipeng Deng, 'Balanced Support Calibrations for Moser's Worm Problem' (arXiv:2609.04591, submitted 2026-09-04), claims a specific isosceles-triangle convex cover of area 0.257883595..., also with Lean 4 code and a Python symbolic replay verifier; this is a weaker (larger-area) upper bound than Keller's and appears to be superseded by it, though the two use different constructions and neither paper is aware of / cites the other given their near-simultaneous posting. Deng has an earlier, related preprint (arXiv:2412.10686, 'A General Solution to Bellman's Lost-in-a-Forest Problem', Dec 2024) proposing a general optimization framework said to extend to Moser's worm problem, but that paper only sketches a methodology and claims no numeric bound on the worm problem itself. None of these three preprints has been digested by a named expert (no Terence Tao blog post, no Quanta Magazine coverage, no journal acceptance found), and neither Keller nor Deng has a discoverable academic footprint tied to this specific subfield (search for 'Zhipeng Deng' turns up several different researchers in unrelated fields; no institutional affiliation is listed on either paper). I found no evidence of AI system involvement in producing either result: neither abstract, comments field, nor (for Keller) the linked GitHub README mentions any AI/LLM tool; both papers use Lean 4 (a proof assistant, not an AI system) and, for Deng, a Python 'exact symbolic replay verifier' (deterministic symbolic/rational-arithmetic code, not machine learning). A search for adjacent AI-mathematics activity turned up a Quanta Magazine piece ('Why the Legendary Erdős Problems Are Falling to AI', Aug 2026) and a GitHub repo named 'clanker-solving-riemman-hypothesis-inator' (an LLM-agent scaffolding project using Claude and Codex) whose issue #142 asks an agent to reconstruct the 2013 Khandhawit–Pagonakis–Sriswasdi lower bound — but that repo explicitly states 'Scaffolding. No mathematical results yet,' and it is unconnected to either the Keller or Deng preprint. Because neither preprint is yet expert-digested, status is 'progress' rather than 'claimed'/'partial'/'resolved' — a bound on an open problem moved, but the problem itself (find the exact infimum area, convex or not) is unchanged and still open.
competing_reading: One could argue Keller's result should be 'claimed' rather than 'progress', since it targets the specific numeric bound the Wikipedia bullet's framing implicitly tracks ('smallest area... that can cover every unit curve') and comes with a machine-checked Lean certificate. I classified it as 'progress' because (a) it is only days old at the time of this research, unpublished, and un-digested by any named expert, and (b) per §6.1 a Lean certificate with no expert reader is only enough for 'claimed', and even 'claimed' felt too strong given zero external commentary exists yet to confirm the certificate is sound (a Lean proof can compile while encoding the wrong statement). If independent verification or expert commentary surfaces, this should move to 'claimed'. Also, both preprints appearing within two weeks of each other and citing no common lineage raises a small possibility that one or both could be retracted or found flawed — worth flagging as an open risk rather than a settled improvement.
what_would_settle_it: An expert digestion (blog post, Quanta piece, or referee report) confirming the Lean formalization in either arXiv:2609.21968 or arXiv:2609.04591 actually encodes the stated theorem and is sound; or a follow-up preprint citing and building on either result; or evidence that one/both have been withdrawn.
